subject: Critical Thinking
title: Opportunity Cost: What You Give Up by Choosing
description: A 60-second lesson on Opportunity Cost: What You Give Up by Choosing.

hook.text: You spend $50,000 on an MBA. The cost isn't $50,000 — it's $50,000 plus two years of salary you didn't earn.

buildup.text: Opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you gave up by making a choice.

discovery.text: Every decision has a visible cost and an invisible cost. Most people only see the visible one.

twist.text: Time is the ultimate opportunity cost. Every hour spent on X is an hour not spent on Y. And you can't get hours back.

climax.text: Good decision-making requires comparing options against each other — not just evaluating them in isolation.

punchline.text: The real cost of anything is what you gave up to get it.

quiz.question: What is opportunity cost?
options: The price tag of a purchase
The value of the best alternative you gave up
The cost of missed opportunities in the past

details.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when making a choice. Every decision has a hidden price: the thing you did not choose. Ignoring opportunity costs leads to systematically poor resource allocation.
details.whyItMatters: People routinely forget to consider what they are giving up, leading to decisions that seem good in isolation but are poor when alternatives are considered.
takeaways: Every choice has a cost equal to the best forgone alternative
Opportunity costs are invisible, which makes them easy to ignore
Explicitly listing alternatives reveals hidden opportunity costs

faq.question: How do you calculate opportunity cost for a practical decision?
faq.answer: Identify your best alternative and its expected value. The opportunity cost of your chosen option is the value of that next-best alternative. For example, the opportunity cost of attending a meeting is whatever productive work you would have done instead.

faq.question: Why do people frequently ignore opportunity costs in everyday choices?
faq.answer: Opportunity costs are abstract and invisible. The thing you did not choose is never experienced, so it feels like nothing was lost. Making alternatives explicit by listing them forces the hidden cost into view.
